ImageDescription.value: The Milky Way arches across this 360-degree panorama of the night sky above the Paranal Observatory, home of ESO’s Very Large Telescope. The Moon is just rising and the zodiacal light shines above it, while the Milky Way stretches across the sky opposite the observatory. To the right in the image and below the arc of the Milky Way, two of our galactic neighbours, the Small and Large Magellanic Clouds, can be seen. The open telescope domes of the world’s most advanced ground-based astronomical observatory are all visible in the image: the four smaller 1.8-metre Aŭiliary Telescopes that can be used together in the interferometric mode, and the four giant 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes. The image was made from 37 individual frames with a total exposure time of about 30 minutes, taken in the early morning hours.

ObjectName.value: Assy-Turgen Observatory against the backdrop of the center of the Milky Way and the star-forming region around Antares

Categories.value: Assy-Turgen Observatory|Self-published work|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation|Milky Way Galaxy over Kazakhstan|Quality night photography in Kazakhstan|Images from Wiki Science Competition 2025 in Kazakhstan|Astronomy images from Wiki Science Competition 2025|Uploaded via Campaign:wsc-kz|National finalists for the Astronomy category from Wiki Science Competition 2025

ImageDescription.value:
Scientific Description: Assy-Turgen Observatory under the Galactic Center

This high-fidelity composite photograph depicts the Assy-Turgen Astrophysical Observatory situated on the Assy Plateau in Kazakhstan, set against the luminous backdrop of the Milky Way’s Galactic Center. Located at an altitude of 2750 meters above sea level in the Trans-Ili Alatau mountains (part of the Northern Tian Shan range), this site is the only high-altitude observatory in Kazakhstan with ideal astroclimatic conditions, characterized by high atmospheric transparency and minimal light pollution.

Technical Methodology and Data Acquisition

The image is a sophisticated multi-row panorama (6x3 grid) captured using a Canon EOS 6D and a vintage Tokina 135mm f/3.5 lens. To counteract the Earth's rotation and allow for long-exposure photography without star trailing, the camera was mounted on an iOptron SkyTracker.

  • Composite Strategy: The data was accumulated over two consecutive nights from a fixed tripod position. The sky portion consists of a 6x2 grid, while the terrestrial foreground uses a 6x1 row.
  • Signal-to-Noise Optimization: Each of the 18 tiles in the panorama is a stack of 6 individual frames. This stacking technique significantly reduces digital noise and enhances the subtle gradients of deep-sky nebulae.
  • Exposure Parameters: Every sub-frame was exposed for 180 seconds at ISO 1600, resulting in a massive total integration time that reveals celestial structures invisible to the naked eye.
  • Post-Processing: The frames were stitched in specialized panoramic software and blended to maintain the geometric integrity between the ground and the celestial sphere.

Astronomical and Astrophysical Highlights

The celestial portion of the image focuses on the most structurally complex region of our galaxy.

  1. The Rho Ophiuchi Cloud Complex: To the right of the main observatory dome, the image captures the vibrant area around Antares in the constellation Scorpius. This region is a stellar nursery containing colorful emission, reflection, and dark nebulae.
  2. The Dark River Nebula: A prominent feature is the "Dark River," a massive lane of cold, dense interstellar dust that obscures the light from stars behind it, stretching from the Pipe Nebula toward the Rho Ophiuchi region.
  3. Galactic Bulge: The dense "star clouds" in the background represent the central bulge of the Milky Way, located approximately 26,000 light-years away.

Terrestrial Context: The Observatory

The foreground provides a detailed look at the infrastructure of the Assy-Turgen Observatory:

  • Main Dome: The large tower houses the 1.5-meter AZT-20 telescope, the observatory's primary instrument.
  • Supporting Structures: To the left is the hotel building for visiting researchers, and to the right is the residential house used by the scientific staff.
  • Geography: The jagged, snow-capped peaks of the Trans-Ili Alatau are visible in the distance, providing a natural horizon that illustrates the extreme elevation of the site.

Scientific Value and Uniqueness

This work is scientifically significant as it documents the atmospheric quality of a critical Eurasian astronomical site.

  • Astroclimatic Record: The clarity with which the 135mm lens resolved the dark nebulae at 180-second exposures serves as an empirical testament to the "seeing" quality at the Assy Plateau.
  • Educational Utility: By combining a high-resolution terrestrial landscape with a deep-sky survey, the image provides a rare perspective on the scale of human scientific endeavors relative to the cosmos.
  • Technological Fusion: The use of a "vintage" 135mm lens for modern digital stacking demonstrates that high-quality astronomical data can be retrieved using a mix of classic optics and contemporary sensor technology.

Key Features for Analysis

When examining this image, one should pay close attention to the transition between the dark dust lanes (The River) and the brilliant star fields. The preservation of the natural colors of the stars—ranging from the deep orange of Antares to the blue-white of young hot stars—indicates a highly successful color calibration that respects the physics of stellar temperatures.

ImageDescription.value:
In mid-August 2010 ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky snapped this photo at ESO’s Paranal Observatory, Chile. A group of astronomers were observing the centre of the Milky Way using the laser guide star facility at Yepun, one of the four Unit Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope (VLT).

Yepun’s laser beam crosses the southern sky and creates an artificial star at an altitude of 90 km high in the Earth's mesosphere. The Laser Guide Star (LGS) is part of the VLT’s adaptive optics system and is used as a reference to correct the blurring effect of the atmosphere on images. The colour of the laser is precisely tuned to energise a layer of sodium atoms found in one of the upper layers of the atmosphere — one can recognise the familiar colour of sodium street lamps in the colour of the laser. This layer of sodium atoms is thought to be a leftover from meteorites entering the Earth’s atmosphere. When excited by the light from the laser, the atoms start glowing, forming a small bright spot that can be used as an artificial reference star for the adaptive optics. Using this technique, astronomers can obtain sharper observations. For example, when looking towards the centre of our Milky Way, researchers can better monitor the galactic core, where a central supermassive black hole, surrounded by closely orbiting stars, is swallowing gas and dust.

Taken with a wide angle lens, this photo covers about 180° of the sky.

ObjectName.value: Night Sky from Hawai‘i and Chile (iotw2225c)

Categories.value: Zodiacal light|Gemini Observatory|Orion Molecular Cloud Complex|Gegenschein|NOIRLab Images|Featured pictures of the Milky Way|Milky Way Galaxy over Hawaii|Milky Way Galaxy over Chile|NOIRLab files uploaded by OptimusPrimeBot|Images by Petr Horálek|Astronomical panoramic photography

ImageDescription.value: This is a composite panorama of the entire night sky taken from the platforms of Gemini South in Chile (left) and Gemini North in Hawai‘i (right). These two telescopes comprise the International Gemini Observatory, a Program of NSF’s NOIRLab. The bright white band streaking from left to right is zodiacal light, created by sunlight scattering off interplanetary dust dispersed throughout the Solar System. This light appears along the pathway of the Sun and planets across the sky, known as the ecliptic, and it's so bright that it can easily be mistaken for light pollution on a dark night. The bright patch of light at the center of the image is directly opposite the Sun in the sky. This spot is the Gegenschein. On the left side of the image you can zoom in to see a rising Jupiter along with Venus (brightest spot on the left), Mars, and Saturn in the middle of the zodiacal light.The dust that produces the zodiacal light and Gegenschein comes from a variety of sources, including comet tails and asteroid collisions. Interestingly, Mars may actually produce a large portion of this dust as it sheds its atmosphere, based on recent studies.This photo was taken as part of the recent NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition to all the NOIRLab sites.

Credit.value: Night Sky from Hawai‘i and Chile

Artist.value: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/ P. Horálek (Institute of Physics in Opava), T. Slovinský

147428729.title: File:Rubin Observatory Under the Milky Way (noirlab2409b).jpg

ObjectName.value: Rubin Observatory Under the Milky Way (noirlab2409b)

Categories.value: Vera C. Rubin Observatory|NOIRLab Images|Milky Way Galaxy over Chile|NOIRLab files uploaded by OptimusPrimeBot

ImageDescription.value: View of Vera C. Rubin Observatory beneath the glittering band of the Milky Way. Rubin Observatory, located in Chile, will use an 8.4-meter telescope equipped with the largest digital camera in the world to conduct a 10-year survey of the entire southern hemisphere sky beginning in late 2025. The resulting data, with images taken through six different color filters, will make it easier than ever for scientists to isolate stellar streams among and beyond the Milky Way and examine them for signs of dark matter disruption.Alt text: Rubin Observatory under a starry night sky. The observatory sits on top of its rocky summit site in the foreground, and is made of a long white building that extends to the left and a silver angular dome sticking up. The Milky Way is visible, spanning the image horizontally above the observatory as a dense stream of stars interspersed with dark and wispy dust clouds. The yellow glow of city lights in La Serena are seen in the distance to the lower left.

Credit.value: Rubin Observatory Under the Milky Way
